b: Running until 17 Nov, the exhibition features interactive installations and furniture designs highlighting sustainable forestry and applications for American hardwoods.
Guests and co-designers at the opening ceremony of the Forested Future exhibition in Shanghai

An exhibition exploring sustainable American hardwoods through interactive installations and furniture design opened in Shanghai on 29 Oct, bringing together artists, designers and home furnishing brands.

Titled Forested Future, the initiative is supported by the American Hardwood Export Council (AHEC) and curated by Cooollect. Inspired by the documentary of the same name, it recreates an urban forest through botanical displays, woodwork, lighting and sound.
iTSLab performed a forest-inspired musical piece at the opening ceremony

Held at the historic Brunner Mond Building on the Bund, the exhibition takes visitors through different stages of a tree’s life, from seed germination and forest management to the use of hardwood in furniture and design. It runs until 17 Nov.
A forest-inspired musical performance by iTSLab, one of the exhibition’s co-creation teams, took place on 27 Oct, ahead of the opening ceremony.

The launch was attended by representatives including Alexander Blamberg, director of the Agricultural Trade Office in Shanghai; John Chan, AHEC regional director for South East Asia and Greater China; and Rupert Oliver, AHEC director of environmental policy.
Artists, designers, representatives from 10 participating home furnishing brands and media organisations also attended.

During the ceremony, guests and co-designers placed leaf-shaped pieces of American hardwood on a forest map to symbolise the role of science-based forest management in maintaining forest health and biodiversity.
Alexander Blamberg, director of the Agricultural Trade Office in Shanghai, at the exhibition
In his opening address, Chan said the exhibition aimed to encourage greater recognition of wood as a material choice.

“Wood is widely acknowledged as the most eco-friendly natural material worldwide,” he said. “The forests that yield American hardwoods are governed by stringent laws, regulations and science-based management frameworks. Forest growth rates consistently outpace harvesting volumes, guaranteeing the continuous accumulation and regeneration of forest resources.”

He noted that available species include red oak, white oak, walnut, cherry, ash and maple. Their range of properties allows designers to select suitable materials for different applications, reducing the need to use scarce alternatives or materials with heavier environmental footprints.
Chan also highlighted timber’s role in carbon storage, explaining that carbon absorbed by trees remains stored in wood when it is used in furniture and architectural applications.

“A tree’s life does not conclude at harvest; instead, it lives on in a new form as part of our daily lives, while continuing to contribute to global carbon reduction. This is the core message we aim to share with every visitor through the exhibition,” he said.
A look at the collaborative installations
The exhibition features installations developed by artists and designers, each exploring a different aspect of the relationship between forests and wood products.
Seeds: Slices by Wang Zi uses American cherry and botanical materials to explore the early stages of a tree’s life
Floral artist Wang Zi’s installation explores seed development through enlarged structures and botanical materials.

Made using American cherry, seeds, fruits, moss, soil and bark, the work features layered forms inspired by the internal structures of seeds. Its base combines natural materials to represent the cycles of growth and decay.
TAG Studio’s Forest Balance uses American white oak and ash in an interactive installation exploring forest management and carbon storage
Multimedia art collective TAG Studio presents Forest Balance, an interactive installation exploring the relationship between forest management, human intervention and carbon storage.

Using the metaphor of weighing scales, the work examines how responsible harvesting can support forest regeneration. One part depicts tree growth alongside the opening of forest areas to encourage new saplings, while another illustrates the movement of carbon and water through the ecosystem.
Visitors can place their hands on the installation’s weighing platforms, becoming part of the work and symbolically acting as both interveners and guardians.
Playing a Tree uses American white oak, ash, maple, cherry and walnut, allowing visitors to activate soundscapes through interaction with hardwood cross-sections
The sound-based installation Playing a Tree draws parallels between tree trunk cross-sections and vinyl records, using wood growth rings as inspiration for its design.

Developed by iTSLab with Zhang Cheng’er and Vinci, the work uses cross-sections of different American hardwood species as interactive sound surfaces. Visitors place their hands on the wood and rotate it to activate forest-inspired soundscapes, with each species producing a different sound.
Visitors can insert ash and maple slats into Hou Zhengguang’s Cave Heaven installation, which is made primarily from American red oak
Designer Hou Zhengguang’s Cave Heaven explores the potential of processed hardwood through an interactive timber structure.

Made primarily from American red oak, the framework features openings of different sizes into which visitors can insert wooden slats made from ash and maple. This allows them to explore the different colours, textures and properties of the species while contributing to the installation’s final form.
The work takes its name from a Taoist concept describing a hidden passage to a self-contained world.
Together, the installations and furniture pieces trace the journey from seed and forest management to timber processing and finished products

Alongside the installations, the exhibition features selected works from 10 home furnishing brands. The pieces use American hardwood species including walnut, ash, white oak and cherry to demonstrate their applications in furniture and interior design.
